summary: Describes Proxy Mobile IPv4, which lets IPv4 devices that lack a Mobile IPv4 client still be handled by the network for mobility, as used in WiMAX Forum and 3GPP2 systems. The network does the signaling on the device's behalf.

eli5.summary: Some devices cannot tell the network when they move. This note has the network do it for them, so they keep their address while roaming.

questions: how does wimax proxy mobile ip work
why do devices need proxy mobility
subtitle: Network-based mobility for IPv4 devices without client software.

tldr.problem: Most IPv4 devices lack Mobile IPv4 client software, so they cannot signal their location when moving between networks, losing their IP address and breaking active connections.
tldr.mechanism: Proxy Mobile IPv4 places the mobility client function in a network element (the Proxy Mobility Agent) that registers on behalf of the device with the Home Agent, tunneling traffic to maintain the device's address.
tldr.outcome: Devices gain mobility support without any software changes or configuration, maintaining their IP address as they roam across networks like WiMAX and 3GPP2 systems.

today: RFC 5563 is Informational and describes Proxy Mobile IPv4 as implemented in WiMAX and 3GPP2 networks. RFC 5213 defined Proxy Mobile IPv6, the IETF standard for network-based mobility with IPv6. PMIPv4 implementations remain in use in deployed WiMAX and cellular systems, though IPv6 and newer protocols are gaining adoption.

sections.title: The Unmodified Device Problem
sections.content:
Mobile IPv4 (defined in RFC 3344) lets a device signal its location to its home network as it moves, maintaining its home IP address and active TCP connections. However, most IPv4 devices—phones, tablets, older laptops—lack Mobile IPv4 client software. Vendors cannot easily add it due to diverse operating systems, closed firmware, or resource constraints.

Proxy Mobile IPv4 solves this by moving the client function into the network. A Proxy Mobility Agent (PMA) in the access network—a base station, access point, or router—performs Mobile IPv4 signaling on the device's behalf. This allows any IPv4 device to gain mobility support without any modification or configuration.
sections.eli5: Instead of the device telling the network where it is, the network watches and tells a central server. The device does not need to know about mobility at all.

sections.title: How Proxy Mobile IPv4 Works
sections.content:
When a mobile device connects to an access network, it authenticates with the access router. The PMA then sends a Proxy Registration Request (PRRQ) to the device's Home Agent (HA), a router on the home network. The PRRQ contains the device's network address (obtained from DHCP or PPP/IPCP) and a tunnel endpoint at the PMA. The HA replies with a Proxy Registration Reply (PRRP), confirming the device's home address and establishing a tunnel.

Once the tunnel is set up, all traffic to and from the mobile device flows through the PMA and HA. The device sees only its home address on its interface, even though it is on a foreign network. When the device moves to a new PMA, the new PMA sends an updated PRRQ with the same home address, and the HA redirects traffic to the new tunnel endpoint. To the device, it appears to stay at home regardless of where it roams.
sections.eli5: The network sees the device attach, tells a home server the device is here, and creates a tunnel. When the device moves, a new network point tells the home server the new location. The device's address never changes.

sections.title: Components and Deployment Models
sections.content:
Proxy Mobile IPv4 consists of several key components. The Proxy Mobility Agent Client (PMIPv4 Client) detects device attachment and initiates registration. The Foreign Agent (FA) is the tunnel endpoint. In an integrated PMA, both functions are collocated in one device like an access router. In a split PMA, the PMIPv4 Client and FA are separate network elements.

The Home Agent is a standard Mobile IPv4 home agent enhanced with PMIPv4 support. It maintains binding entries for each mobile device and tunnels traffic to and from the PMA. The PMA communicates with an Access Router (AR), which typically performs authentication with an AAA (Authentication, Authorization, Accounting) server. DHCP or PPP/IPCP is used to assign and configure the device's IP stack.

Two main deployment scenarios are addressed in this RFC: WiMAX Forum systems, where the PMA may be split across multiple network elements, and 3GPP2 systems used by cellular carriers, where the PMA provides handover support for mobile devices moving between base stations.
sections.eli5: Different parts of the network watch for the device, tell the home server, and manage the tunnel. Different types of networks (WiMAX, cellular) use different setups.

sections.title: Initial Attachment and Mobility
sections.content:
When a device first connects, the PMA detects it and performs authentication with the AAA server. The device then requests an IP address via DHCP or PPP. This triggers the PMA to send a PRRQ. The HA assigns or authorizes a home address and replies with a PRRP. The access router then delivers the assigned address to the device (via DHCP Ack or IPCP Configure-Nak). The device configures its IP stack with this address, which is valid on the home network.

When the device moves to a new PMA, the new PMA performs re-authentication with the AAA server. It then sends a new PRRQ with the device's known home address and the new PMA's tunnel endpoint. The HA updates its binding and redirects traffic to the new tunnel. The device continues using its home address without interruption. The old PMA can send a Registration Revocation to clean up its state, though this is optional.

Periodically, the PMA renews the registration before its lifetime expires, maintaining the tunnel and device connectivity. If the device detaches (loses radio link), the PMA stops renewal and the HA eventually times out the binding.
sections.eli5: Device connects → network gets an address → network tells home server → traffic flows. Device moves → new network tells home server → traffic redirects. Device leaves → home server forgets.

sections.title: Benefits and Use Cases
sections.content:
Proxy Mobile IPv4 brings several benefits. Devices gain mobility without any software installation or reconfiguration, critical for embedded devices or closed systems. Mobility signaling happens on the network, not the air link, reducing traffic and battery drain. The solution works with any access technology (WLAN, cellular, WiMAX) because it uses network-layer tunneling, not link-layer tricks.

Existing Home Agent implementations can serve both client-based Mobile IPv4 and network-based PMIPv4 devices simultaneously, lowering deployment costs. WiMAX networks use PMIPv4 to provide seamless handover between base stations without device involvement. 3GPP2 cellular networks use it to support legacy handsets and optimized handover for high-speed mobility. Some implementations also support IPv6 devices through complementary mechanisms.
sections.eli5: Devices just work without changes. Different networks can use the same server. Phones can hand off between towers without knowing it is happening.
